_podcast.theme_description: Today we explore how Cariboo and BC Indigenous nations are using technology on their own terms — for language revitalization, land stewardship, cultural preservation, and self-determined governance. We're looking for stories that centre Indigenous voices and leadership in innovation, where technology serves community sovereignty rather than replacing it.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Fast Company] Frozen blueberry recall expands to product sold at Walmart as E. coli hospitalizations rise
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Another blueberry product is being recalled due to concerns that it may be contaminated with E. coli.

The latest product is believed to be linked to an ongoing outbreak that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has been investigating since May. This time, the product was available at Walmart. Here’s what you need to know.

What’s happened?

Back in May, the CDC began investigating a multi-state outbreak of E. coli infections. The outbreak was believed to be linked to blueberries.

In early July, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) notified the public about a food recall associated with the outbreak.

As Fast Company reported at the time, that recalled product was Frozen GreenWise Organic IQF Blueberries. It was manufactured by Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A. of San Carlos, Chile, and sold at Publix stores.

Then, in late July, the FDA again notified the public of another blueberry product recall, this one also related to the ongoing E. coli outbreak.

This second recall encompassed four additional GreenWise Organic products containing whole blueberries and whole mixed berries.

Now, yet another product is believed to be linked to the E. coli outbreak, which has expanded to include 17 infections, six of which have required hospitalization.

What additional product is being recalled?

On September 2, Frutas y Hortalizas del Sur S.A. announced a voluntary expansion of its previous recall. The FDA notified the public the next day.

That recall includes a single additional product:

  • Product: Great Value Organic Triple Berry Blend 10 OZ (Including Strawberries, Blackberries and Blueberries), with UPC: 7874211226
  • Package Size: 10 oz
  • Lot Code: 6040 01-6 (in front of the package)
  • Best If Used By Date: February 9, 2028

Where was the recalled product sold?

The recalled Great Value Organic Triple Berry Blend was sold at select Walmart stores in more than a dozen states, according to the recall notice. Those states include:

  • Alabama
  • Arkansas
  • Florida
  • Illinois
  • Indiana
  • Kentucky
  • Louisiana
  • Minnesota
  • Mississippi
  • Missouri
  • North Carolina
  • Ohio
  • Oklahoma
  • South Carolina
  • Texas
  • Wisconsin

What should I do if I have the recalled products?

If you have the recalled product in your possession, you should not consume it. Instead, the recall notice instructs the consumer to dispose of the product or take it back to Walmart for a full refund.

How widespread is the blueberry E. coli outbreak?

According to a September 3 update from the CDC, the outbreak has so far resulted in 17 cases. Six of those individuals have required hospitalization. That’s a hospitalization rate of 35%.

So far, infections related to the outbreak are known to have occurred only in two states: Florida (13 cases) and Georgia (4 cases).

However, the FDA notes that while those infected are so far only from Georgia and Florida, the recalled products believed to be linked to the outbreak were distributed much more widely.

According to the FDA, the recalled products were distributed to the following states:

  • Alabama
  • Arkansas
  • Florida
  • Georgia
  • Illinois
  • Indiana
  • Kentucky
  • Louisiana
  • Minnesota
  • Missouri
  • North Carolina
  • Ohio
  • Oklahoma
  • South Carolina
  • Tennessee
  • Texas
  • Virginia
  • Wisconsin

The CDC says the outbreak investigation is ongoing.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Extreme drought now covers 44% of Puerto Rico
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Puerto Rico’s normally rainy season has instead brought a severe and fast-growing drought. By August 25, three-quarters of the territory was in at least moderate drought, with extreme drought covering 44 percent and some areas receiving less than 20 percent of their usual rainfall. Water shortages have forced rationing, while farmers are losing crops and ranchers are running low on hay. The situation has become serious enough to trigger both local and federal disaster declarations.

🪶 ✏️

The psychedelic compound that makes magic mushrooms so trippy shows serious promise for protecting cancer patients from years of chronic pain. 

For people undergoing cancer treatment, the nerve pain associated with blasting the body with chemotherapy can be debilitating. Even worse, the pain and discomfort can last for years—well after the body is done fighting cancer—and there’s no effective treatment to relieve it. 

Known as peripheral neuropathy, the condition is caused by damage to nerves in the extremities, often the hands, feet, arms, and legs. Clinicians and researchers at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center have found that psilocybin administered to mice prior to dosing them with chemo completely blocks the painful condition from developing. 

Mice in the study received two doses of psilocybin, the compound in mushrooms that causes hallucinations. They then underwent six rounds of chemotherapy lasting six months. Animals in a control group not given psilocybin went on to develop hypersensitivity to pain, a dulled sense of touch in their paws, and “withered” sensory nerve fibers in their skin.

Miraculously, the animals treated with psilocybin made it through chemo without any of the reduced paw sensation or shriveled nerves. The chemotherapy worked just as well to reduce the tumors for mice in the psilocybin test group. 

The results are so compelling that human trials are set to begin this month. Researchers believe that psilocybin is able to protect nerves from damage by keeping energy-generating mitochondria moving along its normal pathways. 

“There is an urgent need for treatments that prevent nerve injury without interfering with lifesaving chemotherapy,” the research group’s coleader, Dr. Moran Amit, said. The groundbreaking research was published this week in Nature.

Lingering long-term pain

Because chemo works systemically, affecting parts of the body well beyond the borders of a patient’s cancer cells, nerve damage can be a painful side effect of the treatment.

More than a third of cancer patients treated with chemotherapy develop peripheral neuropathy. As many as 60% of patients who receive platinum-based chemotherapy, common for shrinking tumors in the ovaries and lungs, experience the painful side effect.

People with peripheral neuropathy describe it as a burning, prickling, or pins-and-needles-like sensation. Such sensations arise when sensory neurons in the outer layers of the skin are damaged, interfering with the way mitochondria travels through them.

“Depleted of energy, the neurons’ tips degenerate, dulling tactile sensation and sparking chronic pain,” the MD Anderson study explains.

Psychedelic renaissance

The breakthrough research on neuropathy is just the latest point of excitement in the cutting edge field of psychedelics research. Psychedelic drugs like psilocybin, long dismissed as purely recreational and blackballed in the medical world, are in the throes of a research renaissance. 

The magic in magic mushrooms has shown promise for treating depression, anxiety, and substance use disorder in recent years, with more research on the way.

In May, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs announced a new clinical trial to evaluate MDMA (commonly known as the party drug Ecstasy or Molly) as a treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder in veterans. 

Beyond psychiatric conditions, the new study in Nature shows that psychedelics could unlock powerful treatments in the broader medical world.

“These findings offer important insights into how psilocybin may protect nerves before damage occurs, rather than treating symptoms after they become persistent,” Amit said. “At UT MD Anderson, we are actively exploring the multiple facets of psychedelics to pursue interventions that improve the lives of our patients.”
